replacement: When I came back two months later, I found the young lady already married to a rich landowner of the neighborhood. He was a very amiable man, still young though older than I was, connected with the best Petersburg society, which I was not, and well educated, which I also was not. I was so overwhelmed by this unexpected blow that my mind was positively clouded. The worst of it was that, as I learned then, the young landowner had been engaged to her for a long time. I had met him many times in her house, but blinded by my conceit I had noticed nothing. And this mortified me most of all: almost everybody had known about it, while I knew nothing. I was filled with sudden, uncontrollable fury. My face burned as I recalled how often I had been on the point of declaring my love to her. She had not tried to stop me or warn me, so I concluded that she must have been laughing at me all the time. Later, of course, I thought it over and remembered that she had been very far from laughing at me. On the contrary, she used to turn aside any love-making of mine with a joke and start talking about other things. But at that moment I could not reflect, and I was all eagerness for revenge. I am surprised, remembering it, that my rage and vengefulness were so extremely repugnant to my own nature. I was easygoing and found it hard to stay angry with anyone for long. So I had to work myself up artificially, and I ended by becoming revolting and absurd.
I was in ecstasy, laughing and chattering all the way. I do not remember about what.
The seconds were shouting too, mine most of all: “Can you disgrace the regiment like this, facing your opponent and begging his pardon! If I had only known!”

I enjoyed listening to them and looking at them. “My dear friends and comrades,” said I, “do not trouble yourselves about my resigning, because I have already done it. I sent in my papers this morning, and as soon as I get my discharge I will enter a monastery. That is why I am leaving the regiment.”

It was the same with the society of the town. Until then I had been received kindly but had attracted no special attention. Now everyone got to know me at once, and everyone invited me. They laughed at me, but they loved me. I should mention that although everybody talked openly about our duel, the authorities paid it no mind. My antagonist was a close relation of our general, and since no blood had been shed and nothing serious had come of it, and since I had resigned my commission, they treated it as a joke. And from then on I began to speak out loud and without fear, regardless of their laughter, for their laughter was always kindly and never spiteful. These conversations mostly took place in the evenings, in the company of ladies. Women especially liked to hear me, and they made the men listen.
